newsitem.title: USA: Dollar ends higher again in U.S., nears 1.80 marks.
newsitem.headline: Dollar ends higher again in U.S., nears 1.80 marks.

text.p: The dollar continued to assault the crumbling mark on Monday, ending U.S. trade just shy of 1.80 marks after a brief bout of profit-taking set up a late surge, dealers said.
A wire story reportedly quoted an anonymous Bundesbank official saying the bank was concerned with the dollar above 1.75 marks, but not enough to intervene to support the mark.
"The dollar was trading at 1.7910 marks when the story came out. It went down to 1.7850 and then it snapped straight back up," said Stephen Jury, chief currency dealer at Union Bank of Switzerland.
The quick flight out of dollars emboldened bargain-hunters and helped the dollar run past stop-loss bids parked near 1.7940 and 1.7960 marks, traders said.
The dollar twice charged toward 1.80 marks, but stopped just shy of the key level, where dealers reported heavy offers.
"The selloff into the London close cleared the slate. If we get through 1.80 marks, clearly we could see some more fireworks," said Bob Savage, chief dealer at Lehman Brothers.
The dollar ended higher at 1.7950/60 marks, up from 1.7895/05 at the open.
Dollar/Swiss rose in sympathy, dealers said, ending at 1.4748/58, up from 1.4738/48. Dollar/yen was little changed at 113.95/05 versus 113.92/02
The dollar's run to fresh six-year highs against the mark drew large support from sterling/mark's continued stay above 3.00, dealers said.
An overnight report showing British producer prices fell further than expected in June failed to slow the sterling/mark juggernaut, dealers said.
But the mark suffered large losses against most other currencies as well, including the Italian lira.
That apparently brought in official support for the German unit. Traders in Europe said the Bank of Italy had bought mark/lira at 970, boosting the mark from a six-month low.
Rumors claimed other authorities had also intervened to bolster the mark, including Scandinavian central banks.
"There were a number of central banks in Europe rumored to be aggressive buyers of marks," said Savage.

Monday's session was the fourteenth consecutive, excluding the July 4 U.S. Independence Day holiday, in which the dollar has posted a new high versus the mark, pointing to further gains ahead, traders said.
"The trend is clear. The dollar should continue upwards for a bit more, though it will be bumpy, as usual," said Christer Stefansson, a mark trader at Swedbank.
The dollar had made sharp gains late Friday, breaching 1.78 marks and capping a strong week that turned many dollar sellers into buyers, traders said.
"Everything was set in place by the price action last week," said Jury.
The mark has slumped recently amid signs Germany may not meet the entry rules for a single European currency while prospects in some typically weaker neighbors are improving.
In the United States, data continue to show a strong economy, drawing funds away from German investments, traders said.
On Monday, the Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta reported its index of manufacturing activity rose in June, keeping alive expectations for higher U.S. interest rates, traders said.
In other trade, the pound slipped to $1.6872/82 from $1.6875/85 at the open. The dollar rose to Canadian $1.3693/98 from C$1.3686/91. The Australian dollar ended at $0.7375/80.
((--Chris Stetkiewicz, 212-859-1664))
